title: The normalized determinant generates the diagonal ideal on each projective-line product chart
statement: Let S be a scheme, P=P1_S, W=P ×_S P, and p1,p2 its projections. Write U_i for the standard open x_i nonzero, and r_ik=x_k/x_i for its coordinate ratios [lem-weil-pbc-projective-space-standard-charts]. For i,j in {0,1} and every affine open V of W contained in p1 inverse(U_i) intersect p2 inverse(U_j), the kernel ideal of the diagonal [def-sbc-closed-immersion-ideal-sheaf] on V is the principal ideal generated by p1*(r_i0)*p2*(r_j1) - p1*(r_i1)*p2*(r_j0), where all functions are restricted to V. There is no reducedness, nonemptiness, or Noetherian hypothesis on S.

source.place: First sentence: the diagonal equation x0*y1-x1*y0=0, expanded on the four standard product charts.

proof.text: Pull the coordinate ratios back along an arbitrary morphism into a product chart. The ratio change formula gives a_ik = a_jk*a_ij for a single projective-space morphism on two charts, and a_ii=1. Consequently the normalized determinant vanishes when the two projections agree. In Lean these are the private pull_ratio_mul and chart_det_zero, using the proved source map_coordRatio_eq_mul and coordRatio_self.

Conversely, let a and b be the two normalized coordinate families. Vanishing of the two-by-two determinant implies a_k*b_i=b_k for k=0,1. Since b_j=1, b_i has inverse a_j. The invertibility of b_i implies that the second morphism also lands in chart i. The coordinate-change formula and cancellation of b_i show equality of all ratios in chart i. Ratio extensionality gives equality of the two morphisms. For arbitrary S first apply the affine-base extensionality theorem after the canonical map to projective space over Spec Z; then use the pullback universal property over S. This is private chart_eq_of_det_zero and chart_hom_ext.

Convert this functorial test into the desired ideal equality. Projective space is proper by lem-pc-projective-proper; the separatedness and closed-diagonal instances make the diagonal a closed immersion, hence its ideal on the affine U is the kernel of its section map. The determinant vanishes under this map by restricting the diagonal to its inverse image of U; this gives the principal-ideal inclusion. For the reverse inclusion let R=Gamma(U), I=(det), and map Spec(R/I) into U and then the product. The determinant is zero under this map, so the preceding test makes its projections equal and factors it through the diagonal. Every section in the diagonal kernel therefore vanishes in R/I, and hence belongs to I. In Lean kernel_ideal_eq_span_of_test implements this argument, using ideal_ker_le and le_ker_comp without any extra quasi-compactness hypothesis on Spec(R/I) to the product. No residue-field or reducedness argument occurs, so zero rings and nilpotents are included.

proof_origin.place: First sentence, the scheme-theoretic determinant equation; proved directly by coordinate-ratio extensionality and the universal quotient test, rather than four affine product-ring identifications.

lean.statement:
theorem p1_diagonal_ideal_on_chart (S : Scheme.{u})
    (i j : ULift.{u} (Fin 2))
    (U : (pullback (ProjectiveLine S ↘ S) (ProjectiveLine S ↘ S)).affineOpens)
    (hi : U.1 ≤ pullback.fst (ProjectiveLine S ↘ S) (ProjectiveLine S ↘ S) ⁻¹ᵁ
      standardOpen (ULift.{u} (Fin 2)) S i)
    (hj : U.1 ≤ pullback.snd (ProjectiveLine S ↘ S) (ProjectiveLine S ↘ S) ⁻¹ᵁ
      standardOpen (ULift.{u} (Fin 2)) S j) :
    (pullback.diagonal (ProjectiveLine S ↘ S)).ker.ideal U =
      Ideal.span {((pullback.fst (ProjectiveLine S ↘ S) (ProjectiveLine S ↘ S)).appLE _ U.1 hi
          (coordRatio (ULift.{u} (Fin 2)) S i ⟨0⟩)) *
        ((pullback.snd (ProjectiveLine S ↘ S) (ProjectiveLine S ↘ S)).appLE _ U.1 hj
          (coordRatio (ULift.{u} (Fin 2)) S j ⟨1⟩)) -
        ((pullback.fst (ProjectiveLine S ↘ S) (ProjectiveLine S ↘ S)).appLE _ U.1 hi
          (coordRatio (ULift.{u} (Fin 2)) S i ⟨1⟩)) *
        ((pullback.snd (ProjectiveLine S ↘ S) (ProjectiveLine S ↘ S)).appLE _ U.1 hj
          (coordRatio (ULift.{u} (Fin 2)) S j ⟨0⟩))}
